title: Al-Karim, the Most Generous
hookLine: the Most Generous, who gives before asked
tomorrow: Amira has a paragraph typed about Kayla. does she send it?

cards: Cardamom tea already on the stove when you walk in. A plate already set at your spot. Some people give before the asking even starts.
Amira's Dadi is one of them. After the campus visit, Amira opened her backpack and found an envelope she never asked for, in Dadi's careful handwriting: for the trip. Forty dollars, folded twice.
She stood in the hallway holding it for a long minute, not sure whether to laugh or cry. The Qur'an has a Name for a giver like that, and it arrives inside a question.

teach.b: Surah Al-Infitar asks: "O man! What hath made thee careless concerning thy Lord, the Bountiful". That last word is today's Name: Al-Karim, the Most Generous. The question is gentle and sharp at once.
With a Lord this generous, how did you stop noticing? The verse doesn't scold. It asks.
Scholars of the Names describe al-Karim as the one who gives before being asked, and gives more than was hoped for. Not a giver who pays back what you earned.
A giver who moves first, like tea on the stove before you've said you're hungry. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: SHY TO SEND HANDS BACK EMPTY.
teach.b: A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi says your Lord is shy and generous: He is shy, when a servant raises their hands to Him, to send them back empty. Shy. A generosity that would be embarrassed to say no.
And karim isn't only a Name.

teach.h: A NOBLE MESSENGER, A NOBLE QUR'AN.
teach.b: The Qur'an uses the same word for things it honors: a noble messenger, a generous reward, and the Qur'an itself, a noble recitation. Generosity here isn't about size.
It's about direction. It moves toward you before you move. That's why an envelope in a backpack can say more than the money inside it.
It says: someone saw what you needed before you said it.

how: Muslims call on Allah as al-Karim in du'a, often with hands raised, and the hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi about a Lord too generous to send raised hands back empty is a well-known encouragement to ask.

o: the Most Generous, who gives before you ask
the one who repays every debt exactly
the one who rewards only hard workers

games.q: the generous ones — tap the pairs.
p: what made you careless of your Lord?

s: a generous giver waits until someone asks
scholars describe al-Karim as giving before being asked, and more than was hoped.
a hadith says God is shy to send raised hands back empty
in the Qur'an, karim describes only God
the same word honors a noble messenger, a generous reward, and the Qur'an itself.

games.q: your friend's car broke down. she needs rides to work all week but she's too proud to ask. what fits al-Karim?
o: text first: 'heading your way at 8 tomorrow. want a ride?'
wait until she asks, so she doesn't feel embarrassed.
offer to cover the repair, as long as she pays you back.
games.why: al-Karim's generosity moves first, before the ask. the other two are kind-ish, but they keep the gift waiting on her pride or on a deal.

practice: Find one small thing you could give: a snack, a pen, a book you've finished, a few dollars. Hold it in your hand and feel its weight.
Think of who might need it before they'd ever ask, then set it by the door or in your bag, ready to go. Let the sit begin with your hands open and empty.

wordCard.voice: Al-Karim. The Most Generous, who gives before the asking, and is shy to send raised hands back empty. Name forty-two.

orig.note: Arabic: the Most Generous, the Noble. in 82:6 it's the Lord you shouldn't grow careless of.

carryVoice: Your line: generous, the gift that arrives before the ask, and the thanks that follows it. Day ninety of the year.
